Lesson 1 · Understand the problem

Which reported stockouts are real?

The chain wants fewer empty shelves without paying for unnecessary inventory. Our first job is to establish what the operating reports actually measure.

Baseline · weeks 1–8 · all 150 stores

Method in this decision: Data origins, quality, organization, and preparation

Read here or present the same material, one step at a time.

The decision brief

The operations director is considering replenishment alerts: a weekly message that asks a store to review low-stock products and bring forward replenishment. Before funding a trial, the director asks how much of the current stockout problem is real. The export has duplicated records, blank counts, and impossible values. The immediate deliverable is a reconciled store-week file with one consistent stockout measure. This file will become the baseline used throughout the course.

Begin with the decision and the evidence

The first approval is for the data

  • Decision: should the chain test replenishment alerts?
  • Evidence needed: a comparable measure of shelf availability.
  • Deliverable: a documented baseline that another analyst can reproduce.

The director’s question gives the preparation work a purpose. Each choice—what to collect, whom to include, how to combine records—changes the evidence available for the spending decision. This lesson follows that chain from a source record to a review table.

What you should be able to do

  • Explain where a dataset came from and whom it represents.
  • Choose observations, variables, measurement scales, and keys.
  • Reshape, join, clean, aggregate, and validate the records.
  • Explain the business measure and reproduce the handover.

Treat these skills as stages of one management deliverable. By the end of the lesson, another analyst should be able to reconstruct the stockout baseline and explain why its rows, denominator, and repair decisions fit the director’s question.

Different sources answer different operating questions

Choose the source to fit the decision
SourceRetail useCollection choice
Systems and APIsSales, orders, delivery logsWhat event triggers a record?
Web recordsCompetitor prices and availabilityWhich products and times are visible?
Administrative recordsStore registry and staffingHow are openings and changes recorded?
Surveys and interviewsStaff explanations of replenishmentWho answers, and how is the question asked?
ExperimentsTest an alert policyWho receives the offer, and when?

A transaction records an event the system was designed to capture. A survey records an answer to a question. An experiment changes an operating rule and measures what follows. Combine these sources deliberately: agreeing on a source is part of defining the business question, not simply a file-format choice.

Six questions make quality concrete

Agree the measurement protocol
QuestionApply it to shelf availability
MeaningDoes a stockout mean unavailable on the shelf or absent from the warehouse?
ValidityDoes this measure the customer-facing availability we want to improve?
ReliabilityWould two reviewers applying the rule obtain similar counts?
ComparabilityAre products, days, and counting rules consistent across stores?
CoverageWhich stores, products, and trading days are represented?
SelectionAre the stores that fail to report systematically different?

Use these questions to assign work. Operations defines “unavailable”; the data team checks coverage; reviewers reconcile disagreements. A polished chart becomes useful only after the underlying measurement agreement is clear. This is the practical meaning of “garbage in, garbage out.”

Begin with the shelf opportunity

Each store follows the same 20 products over seven days. That creates 140 scheduled product-days per store-week. One stockout product-day means one of those products was unavailable on that day. It is a count of shelf availability, not a count of customers or units of lost sales.

The key is the pair store_id and week. A store appears in several weeks, and a week contains many stores. Read the rows below as repeated observations on stores. This distinction will matter again when we estimate uncertainty and evaluate an alert policy assigned to whole stores.

First five reconciled records

Decide which business the file describes

Population, sample, and reporting frame

  • Population: the stores and periods covered by the management question.
  • Frame: the list from which observations can be collected.
  • Sample: the observations actually selected and received.

For the baseline, the target is all 150 stores over eight weeks. That implies 1,200 expected store-week keys. The fixed basket contains 20 monitored products; the measure describes that basket. Lesson 3 later selects 30 stores for a fresh audit, which introduces a sampling question rather than changing the baseline definition.

More rows cannot repair a missing part of the business

  • Coverage: compare the store list with the operating registry.
  • Nonresponse: compare received and scheduled reports.
  • Benchmark: compare location and delivery-time composition.
  • Random sampling: select from the intended frame with known chances.

Imagine that only stores with reliable scanners send a weekly report. Repeatedly collecting their data adds rows without adding the missing stores. The remedy is to improve collection or define the covered population clearly. For an audit, random selection addresses the selection stage; following up selected stores addresses nonresponse.

The four Vs become operating requirements

Plan for scale
DimensionRetail implication
VolumeMore products and stores require efficient storage and checking.
VelocityAlerts need information before the replenishment decision.
VarietyJoin structured counts with logs, text reports, and supplier records.
VeracityKeep definitions, source checks, and an audit trail consistent.

Large datasets are valuable when they make the decision more timely or more informative. Start with what the extra data will change, then weigh collection, storage, access, and review costs. Obtain the right permissions and collect only the information needed for the operating purpose.

Make the table match the question

Three structures, one continuing business

Recognize the observation structure
StructureOne rowQuestion
Cross-sectionalOne store at a specified timeWhich stores differ?
Time seriesOne chain-wide weekHow does the chain change over time?
PanelOne store in one weekHow do the same stores change?

A table has observations in rows and variables in columns. Our operating file is a panel. Aggregating across stores produces a chain time series; selecting one week produces a cross-section. These are different views of the same records, each suited to a different question.

Measurement scales determine useful arithmetic

Interpret the values before calculating
ScaleRetail exampleUseful operation
NominalStore ID or location categoryCounts and group comparisons
OrdinalLow, medium, high review priorityOrdering; category shares
IntervalA temperature measured in °CDifferences; zero is not absence of heat
RatioStockout counts or delivery durationDifferences and meaningful ratios

A numeric label is not necessarily a quantity: averaging store IDs has no business meaning. Priority labels have an order, but the distance between “low” and “medium” need not equal the distance to “high.” A count has a genuine zero. Temperature and priority are illustrations of measurement scales, not additional fields in the stockout file.

Choose a practical storage format

Formats serve the same documented variables
FormatUse
CSV or TSVExchange a plain table; document delimiter, encoding, and missing-value codes.
SpreadsheetInspect tables and maintain a small data dictionary.
JSON or XMLRepresent nested records returned by systems or APIs.
ParquetStore large typed tables efficiently in columns.

The file extension does not tell you the observation unit or what a blank means. Preserve a source description and a variable dictionary beside the data. Record collector, purpose, dates, field definitions, units, category codes, allowed ranges, and transformations.

Inspect before filtering

import pandas as pd
raw = pd.read_csv('raw-baseline.csv')
raw.head()
raw.shape
raw.dtypes
raw.isna().sum()

A DataFrame is the table; a Series is one column. head shows example rows, shape reports rows and columns, dtypes shows storage types, and isna counts missing values. Download the CSV from Data & labs for this loading example. The self-contained notebook creates the identical input in its shared setup.

Select columns and rows for explicit reasons

working = raw[['store_id', 'week', 'exposure', 'stockout_days']]
first_weeks = working.loc[working['week'] <= 2]
working.iloc[:3]

A list of names selects columns. loc applies a row rule using labels or a condition; iloc selects by position. Record the before-and-after dimensions when restricting a sample. For categories, value_counts(dropna=False) shows missing labels as well as known groups. Text filters distinguish “Urban” from “urban ” until a documented coding rule reconciles them.

A tidy table has an explicit key

  • One variable per column; one observation per row.
  • Keep different observation types in related tables.
  • Store table key: store_id.
  • Weekly table key: store_id + week.

Identifiers should be present, stable, and unique at the chosen level. Repeated store IDs are expected in a weekly panel. Repeated store-week keys need investigation. Keep an entity crosswalk when two systems use different names for the same store; do not guess that similar names must identify the same location.

Test the proposed identifier

key = ['store_id', 'week']
missing_keys = raw[key].isna().any(axis=1)
duplicate_keys = raw.duplicated(key, keep=False)
raw.loc[missing_keys | duplicate_keys]

Inspect duplicate-key groups before removing rows. Identical repeated exports can be deduplicated; conflicting counts require a source decision. This export contains known repeated records, and the repair ledger supplies the counts for the flagged observations.

Reconcile the export before calculating a rate

The initial export contains 1212 rows. Removing 12 duplicate store-week records leaves 1200. A range check finds 12 records with blank or negative stockout counts. The transaction ledger supplies the corrected counts for those exact keys, preserving all 1200 scheduled store-weeks.

Reconciliation is different from discarding inconvenient rows. An empty count is sent back to its source; a genuine zero remains a valid observation. The repair log records the store, week, and recovered count. A colleague can therefore check how the same store-week moved from the export to the analysis.

Show the same observations in a useful layout

Long format keeps the observation in a row

Two stores, two weeks
StoreWeekStockout daysExposure
S001118140
S00129140
S002112140
S00229140

The store-week key is visible in long form. Adding another week means adding rows. This layout is convenient for joining attributes, grouping, plotting time, and fitting the models later in the course.

Wide format makes a small review table

The same four observations in wide form
Storestockout_days_1stockout_days_2exposure_1exposure_2
S001189140140
S002129140140

Wide form places weeks across columns, which can help a manager compare adjacent periods. The information has not changed. Column names now combine a variable with a week, so return to a long structure when the analysis needs one store-week per row.

Set the key, unstack the week, name the columns

small = clean.query("store_id in ['S001','S002'] and week <= 2")
wide = small.set_index(['store_id','week'])[['stockout_days','exposure']]
wide = wide.unstack('week')
wide.columns = [f'{variable}_{week}' for variable, week in wide.columns]

The two column levels after unstack are variable and week. The naming rule makes both visible, for example stockout_days_2. For a one-variable wide table, melt moves week columns back into rows. Validate row keys and totals after either transformation; reshaping should preserve the measured information.

Join tables without changing what a row means

Choose the relationship before choosing the command

Keys determine the join
RelationshipExampleExpected result
One-to-oneStore profile + store contact recordOne row per store
Many-to-oneWeekly records + store profileOne row per store-week
One-to-manyOne store + its weekly recordsSeveral rows per store
Many-to-manyWeekly records + multiple staffing spellsCandidate pairs; apply the time rule

A foreign key links a row to a record in another table. A left join preserves the weekly file while bringing in store attributes. An inner join retains only matching keys. Review unmatched records before choosing whether the analytical population should shrink.

Make a many-to-one join prove its claim

stores = world()['stores'][['store_id','lead_days','urban']]
joined = clean.merge(stores, on='store_id', how='left',
    validate='many_to_one', indicator=True)
assert len(joined) == len(clean)
assert joined['_merge'].eq('both').all()

The join retains 1,200 store-weeks. validate checks uniqueness on the store side; indicator reveals unmatched rows. Together with the row-count check, these tests prevent a duplicated store profile from silently multiplying the weekly observations.

Responsibility also has a time key

Illustrative staffing ledger for two case stores
StoreManagerFirst weekLast week
S001M0114

This small staffing exercise adds an explicit assignment period. S001 changes manager after week 4. Joining only on store_id produces a candidate row for each possible manager. Retain the candidate whose assignment covers the observation week. The exercise ledger does not change the course’s stockout outcomes.

Use the assignment dates, then recheck uniqueness

Responsibility around the handover
StoreWeekResponsible managerStockout days
S0013M0116

24 candidate pairs → 16 valid store-week assignments

A manager can work at several stores or in several periods, so manager_id alone is not a unique staffing-spell key. After the time condition, every included store-week should have exactly one responsible manager. Record gaps or overlapping assignments for review.

An event and an observation need not be the same thing

Illustrative stock-transfer ledger, viewed by store
TransferWeekStoreDirectionSigned units
T0012S002In6
T0012S001Out-6
T0023S003In4
T0023S002Out-4

Two transfers create four valid store-perspective rows: one outgoing and one incoming for each event. The key is transfer_id plus store_id. Removing the second occurrence of a transfer ID would destroy a valid observation. Signed units sum to zero across the chain, providing an additional reconciliation check.

Build a review table at the level of the decision

Grouping changes the observation unit

reports = pd.DataFrame(preparation_examples()['reports'])
summary = reports.groupby('store_id').agg(
    weeks=('week','size'), stockouts=('stockout_days','sum'),
    exposure=('exposure','sum'))
summary['rate'] = 100 * summary.stockouts / summary.exposure

This demonstration deliberately takes incomplete submissions from six stores. It leaves the full baseline intact. groupby collects each store’s records; named aggregation counts reporting weeks and adds stockouts and exposure. The output has one row per store, so its key and interpretation have changed.

Show the amount of evidence beside the ranking

Incomplete-submission exercise, sorted from lower to higher stockout rate
StoreWeeks receivedStockoutsExposureRate (%)
S0022212807.50
S00111814012.86
S0058157112014.02
S0038159112014.20
S0048164112014.64
S0068174112015.54

A rate based on one week can move sharply with that week’s events. A review rule requiring at least six weeks makes the reporting requirement explicit. It changes eligibility, so name the resulting shortlist as “stores with at least six reported weeks,” rather than calling it the best stores in the chain.

Apply the eligibility rule before plotting

eligible = summary.loc[summary['weeks'] >= 6]
ranked = eligible.sort_values('rate')
ranked[['weeks','rate']]

For a horizontal bar chart, put the store labels on one axis and the stockout rate on the other, using a shared zero and meaningful units. The chart should describe observed service performance. Delivery conditions, product mix, and the length of observation help explain that performance; later lessons compare those conditions directly.

Keep the denominator attached to the result

Across the reconciled file there are 21,407 stockout product-days out of 168,000 scheduled product-days. Dividing the totals gives a baseline rate of 12.74%. A rate puts stores on a common scale; the raw count alone would make a longer reporting period appear worse.

Every store-week has the same 140 opportunities in this case. That makes the mean of store-week rates equal to the rate from pooled counts. If a store later expands its monitored product range, the denominator must travel with the count so that the next report still answers the same question.

The initial business target is a rate at or below 10%. That is a management choice about service, not a statistical estimate. It gives us something useful to compare with the baseline while the financial case for alerts is developed.

Hand over a reproducible piece of evidence

Preserve, profile, define, clean, validate, document

  • Preserve the raw export and its collection notes.
  • Profile types, missing values, ranges, and category counts.
  • Define scope, observation, keys, and business rules.
  • Reconcile values and relationships; record each decision.
  • Validate keys, counts, ranges, join coverage, and totals.

Deletion and imputation are analytical choices. Restricting to complete records changes who remains; filling a missing count adds a value under an explicit rule or model. In this case the ledger lets us recover flagged counts. When recovery is impossible, compare reasonable alternatives and report how the choice changes the decision measure.

Give the project a readable structure

retail-analysis/
  README.txt
  raw/        # original exports and variable dictionary
  clean/      # reconciled tables and repair log
  analysis/   # scripts, figures, and decision memo

Use predictable names such as 2026-11-09_store-week_baseline.csv, stable lower-case field names, and zero-padded sequence numbers when order matters. Separate input paths from output paths. A colleague should be able to find the collection rules and run the pipeline without guessing which file is authoritative.

Use AI to accelerate work that can be checked

  • Ask for code that implements a stated business rule.
  • Inspect the changed rows and reconcile before-and-after totals.
  • Keep the original inputs and an executable audit trail.
  • Have a person approve definitions, exceptions, and the decision.

AI can suggest a reshape or a join quickly. The analyst still decides what counts as a stockout, which two names refer to the same store, and which staffing period applies. Reviewing these choices is part of the work, not a final decorative check. No fixed percentage of project time is assumed here.

Diagnose before cleaning

  • Repeated stores, transfers, and joined rows: which are errors?
Discuss, then reveal

Start from the observation definition. Eight store-week rows can be valid; two transfer-perspective rows can be valid. The staffing join needs its period condition and a uniqueness check. Remove only verified repeated records, not every repeated identifier.

A store appears eight times, a transfer appears twice, and a staffing join doubles the row count. Which records should be removed?

Create the first entry in the decision memo

Hand over the reconciled file together with its key, rate definition, and repair log. The next analyst should be able to join store attributes to it without multiplying rows. The store table has one row per store; the weekly table has one row per store-week. A many-to-one join is the intended operation.

The director can now ask where the problem is concentrated. A chain-wide percentage establishes scale, but the next spending decision will depend on which stores face the largest operational burden. We carry the repaired rows into Lesson 2 rather than starting with a new dataset.

Update the decision memo

Baseline established: 1,200 store-weeks, a fixed denominator of 140 product-days, and a stockout rate of 12.74%. Use this reconciled file for comparisons; retain the source and repair log with it.

Make the call

A blank stockout count appears in a week with 140 scheduled product-days. What enters the rate calculation?

Compare your reasoning

Recover the count from the ledger before calculating the rate. A blank is unresolved information; the denominator is still 140. The recovered count and the reason for repair stay in the log.

The bigger picture

A useful business metric is an agreement about what is counted, over which opportunities, and for which decision. Making those choices visible lets several teams use the same evidence. Here the agreement turns a messy export into the common starting point for every subsequent lesson.

After your decision: open the known answer

The export was created by adding 12 duplicate rows, eight blank counts, and four negative counts to the baseline. Reconciliation recovers the original 1,200 store-weeks exactly.
